In mathematics, '''Hiptmair–Xu (HX) preconditioners'''<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hiptmair |first1=Ralf |last2=Xu |first2=Jinchao |date=2007-01-01 |title={Nodal auxiliary space preconditioning in $backslash$bf H($backslash$bf curl) and $backslash$bf H($backslash$rm div)} spaces |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/257297555 |access-date=2020-07-06 |website=SIAM J. Numer. Anal. |pages=2483 |doi=10.1137/060660588}}</ref> are preconditioners for solving <math>H(\operatorname{curl})</math> and <math>H(\operatorname{div})</math> problems based on the auxiliary space preconditioning framework.<ref>J.Xu, The auxiliary space method and optimal multigrid preconditioning techniques for unstructured grids. Computing. 1996;56(3):215–35.</ref>  An important ingredient in the derivation of HX preconditioners in two and three dimensions is the so-called regular decomposition, which decomposes a [[Sobolev space]] function into a component of higher regularity and a scalar or vector potential. The key to the success of HX preconditioners is the discrete version of this decomposition, which is also known as HX decomposition.  The discrete decomposition decomposes a discrete Sobolev space function into a discrete component of higher regularity, a discrete scale or vector potential, and a high-frequency component.

HX preconditioners have been used for accelerating a wide variety of solution techniques, thanks to their highly scalable parallel implementations, and are known as AMS<ref>T. V. Kolev, P. S. Vassilevski, Parallel auxiliary space AMG for H (curl) problems. Journal of Computational Mathematics. 2009 Sep 1:604–23.</ref> and ADS<ref>T.V. Kolev, P.S. Vassilevski. Parallel auxiliary space AMG solver for H(div) problems. SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing. 2012;34(6):A3079–98.</ref> precondition.  HX preconditioner was identified by the [[United States Department of Energy|U.S. Department of Energy]] as one of the top ten breakthroughs in computational science<ref>Report of The Panel on Recent Significant Advancements in Computational Science, https://science.osti.gov/-/media/ascr/pdf/program-documents/docs/Breakthroughs_2008.pdf</ref> in recent years. Researchers from Sandia, Los Alamos, and Lawrence Livermore National Labs use this algorithm for modeling fusion with magnetohydrodynamic equations.<ref>E.G. Phillips, J. N. Shadid, E.C. Cyr, S.T. Miller, Enabling Scalable Multifluid Plasma Simulations Through Block Preconditioning. In: van Brummelen H., Corsini A., Perotto S., [[Gianluigi Rozza|Rozza G.]] (eds) Numerical Methods for Flows. Lecture Notes in Computational Science and Engineering, vol 132. Springer, Cham 2020.</ref> Moreover, this approach will also be instrumental in developing optimal iterative methods in structural mechanics, electrodynamics, and modeling of complex flows.

==HX preconditioner for <math>H(\operatorname{curl})</math>==

Consider the following  <math>H(\operatorname{curl})</math> problem: Find <math>u \in H_h(\operatorname{curl})</math>  such that

<math> (\operatorname{curl}~u, \operatorname{curl}~v) + \tau (u, v) = (f, v), \quad \forall v \in H_h(\operatorname{curl}), </math> with <math>\tau > 0</math>.

The corresponding matrix form is

<math>
A_{\operatorname{curl}} u  = f.
</math>

The HX preconditioner for <math>H(\operatorname{curl})</math> problem is defined as

<math>
B_{\operatorname{curl}} = S_{\operatorname{curl}} + \Pi_h^{\operatorname{curl}} \, A_{vgrad}^{-1} \, (\Pi_h^{\operatorname{curl}})^T + \operatorname{grad} \, A_{\operatorname{grad}}^{-1} \, (\operatorname{grad})^T,
</math>

where <math> S_{\operatorname{curl}} </math> is a smoother (e.g., Jacobi smoother,  Gauss–Seidel smoother), <math> \Pi_h^{\operatorname{curl}} </math> is the canonical interpolation operator for <math> H_h(\operatorname{curl})</math> space, <math> A_{vgrad}</math> is the matrix representation of discrete vector Laplacian defined on <math> [H_h(\operatorname{grad})]^n</math>,<math>grad</math> is the discrete gradient operator, and <math>A_{\operatorname{grad}}</math> is the matrix representation of the discrete scalar Laplacian defined on <math>H_h(\operatorname{grad})</math>.  Based on auxiliary space preconditioning framework, one can show that

<math>
\kappa(B_{\operatorname{curl}} A_{\operatorname{curl}}) \leq C,
</math>

where <math>\kappa(A)</math> denotes the [[condition number]] of matrix <math>A</math>.

In practice, inverting <math>A_{vgrad}</math> and <math>A_{grad}</math> might be expensive, especially for large scale problems.  Therefore, we can replace their inversion by spectrally equivalent approximations, <math>B_{vgrad}</math> and <math>B_{\operatorname{grad}}</math>, respectively. And the HX preconditioner for <math>H(\operatorname{curl})</math> becomes
<math>
B_{\operatorname{curl}} = S_{\operatorname{curl}} + \Pi_h^{\operatorname{curl}} \, B_{vgrad} \, (\Pi_h^{\operatorname{curl}})^T + \operatorname{grad}  B_{\operatorname{grad}} (\operatorname{grad})^T.
</math>

==HX Preconditioner for <math>H(\operatorname{div})</math>==
Consider the following <math>H(\operatorname{div})</math> problem: Find <math>u \in H_h(\operatorname{div})</math>

<math>(\operatorname{div} \,u, \operatorname{div} \,v) + \tau (u, v) = (f, v), \quad \forall v \in H_h(\operatorname{div}),</math> with <math>\tau > 0</math>.

The corresponding matrix form is

<math>A_{\operatorname{div}} \,u  = f.</math>

The HX preconditioner for <math>H(\operatorname{div})</math> problem is defined as

<math>B_{\operatorname{div}} = S_{\operatorname{div}} + \Pi_h^{\operatorname{div}} \, A_{vgrad}^{-1} \, (\Pi_h^{\operatorname{div}})^T + \operatorname{curl} \, A_{\operatorname{curl}}^{-1} \, (\operatorname{curl})^T,</math>

where <math>S_{\operatorname{div}}</math> is a smoother (e.g., Jacobi smoother,  Gauss–Seidel smoother), <math>\Pi_h^{\operatorname{div}}</math> is the canonical interpolation operator for <math>H(\operatorname{div})</math> space, <math>A_{vgrad}</math> is the matrix representation of discrete vector Laplacian defined on <math>[H_h(\operatorname{grad})]^n</math>, and <math>\operatorname{curl}</math> is the discrete curl operator.

Based on the auxiliary space preconditioning framework, one can show that

<math>\kappa(B_{\operatorname{div}} A_{\operatorname{div}}) \leq C.</math>

For <math>A_{\operatorname{curl}}^{-1}</math> in the definition of <math>B_{\operatorname{div}}</math>, we can replace it by the HX preconditioner for <math>H(\operatorname{curl})</math> problem, e.g., <math>B_{\operatorname{curl}}</math>, since they are spectrally equivalent. Moreover, inverting <math>
A_{vgrad}</math> might be expensive and we can replace it by a spectrally equivalent approximations <math>
B_{vgrad}</math>. These leads to the following practical HX preconditioner for <math>H(\operatorname{div})</math> problem,

<math>B_{\operatorname{div}} = S_{\operatorname{div}} + \Pi_h^{\operatorname{div}} B_{vgrad}  (\Pi_h^{\operatorname{div}})^T + \operatorname{curl}  B_{\operatorname{curl}}  (\operatorname{curl})^T 
 =  S_{\operatorname{div}} + \Pi_h^{\operatorname{div}}  B_{vgrad}  (\Pi_h^{\operatorname{div}})^T + \operatorname{curl}  S_{\operatorname{curl}}  (\operatorname{curl})^T + \operatorname{curl}  \Pi_h^{\operatorname{curl}} B_{vgrad}  (\Pi_h^{\operatorname{curl}})^T  (\operatorname{curl})^T.
</math>

==Derivation==
The derivation of HX preconditioners is based on the discrete regular decompositions for <math>H_h(\operatorname{curl})</math> and <math>H_h(\operatorname{div})</math>, for the completeness, let us briefly recall them.

'''Theorem:'''[Discrete regular decomposition for <math>H_h(\operatorname{curl})</math>]

Let <math>\Omega</math> be a simply connected bounded domain. For any function <math>v_h\in H_h(\operatorname{curl} \Omega)</math>, there exists a vector<math>\tilde{v}_h\in H_h(\operatorname{curl} \Omega)</math>, <math>\psi_h\in [H_h (\operatorname{grad} \Omega)]^3</math>, <math>p_h\in H_h(\operatorname{grad} \Omega)</math>, such that
<math>v_h=\tilde{v}_h+\Pi_h^{\operatorname{curl}}\psi_{h}+ \operatorname{grad} p_h</math> and<math>\Vert h^{-1} \tilde{v}_h\Vert + \Vert\psi_h\Vert_1 + \Vert p_h\Vert_1 \lesssim \Vert v_{h}\Vert_{H(\operatorname{curl})}</math>

'''Theorem:'''[Discrete regular decomposition for <math>H_{h}(\operatorname{div})</math>]
Let <math>\Omega</math> be a simply connected bounded domain. For any function <math>v_{h}\in H_{h}(\operatorname{div} \Omega)</math>, there exists a vector <math>
\widetilde{v}_h\in H_h(\operatorname{div} \Omega)</math>
, <math>\psi_h\in [H_h(\operatorname{grad} \Omega)]^{3},</math> <math>
w_h\in H_h(\operatorname{curl} \Omega),</math>
such that
<math>
	v_{h}=\widetilde{v}_h+\Pi_h^{\operatorname{div}}\psi_h+ \operatorname{curl} \, w_h,
</math>
	and
<math>
	\Vert h^{-1}\widetilde{v}_h\Vert + \Vert\psi_h\Vert_1 + \Vert w_h\Vert_1 \lesssim \Vert v_h \Vert_{H(\operatorname{div})} 
</math>

Based on the above discrete regular decompositions, together with the auxiliary space preconditioning framework, we can derive the HX preconditioners for <math>
H(\operatorname{curl})</math> and <math>H(\operatorname{div})</math> problems as shown before.
